subject: Immunology
vignette: A 52-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. He has ascites, spider angiomata, and marked splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 62,000/mm3 and hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL with a reticulocyte count of 2.1%; the blood smear shows no schistocytes, and direct antiglobulin testing is negative.
question: Which of the following best explains his cytopenias?

options.text: Sequestration and macrophage-mediated destruction of blood cells in the red pulp of an enlarged spleen
Failure of white pulp germinal centers to produce platelets
Autoimmune destruction confined to the splenic marginal zone
Thymic atrophy with loss of T cell help for hematopoiesis
Reduced erythropoietin production by splenic macrophages

explanation_correct: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis causes splenic congestion and enlargement, and the red pulp (splenic cords and sinusoids) then sequesters and destroys blood cells, producing thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia with a normal or only mildly increased reticulocyte count. The red pulp is the blood-filtering compartment, containing cords of macrophages and venous sinuses through which erythrocytes pass slowly. A negative direct antiglobulin test and absence of schistocytes help exclude immune hemolysis and microangiopathic hemolysis.

explanation_incorrect.B: The white pulp is a lymphoid compartment and does not produce platelets; platelets are made by bone marrow megakaryocytes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypersplenic cytopenias are due to mechanical sequestration in the red pulp, not autoimmune destruction confined to the marginal zone.
explanation_incorrect.D: T cell help is not the mechanism of cytopenias here, and the normal reticulocyte count does not suggest marrow failure from loss of T cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney, not by splenic macrophages.

educationalObjective: Hypersplenism from portal hypertension causes cytopenias through red pulp sequestration and macrophage-mediated destruction of blood cells.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has never undergone splenectomy but has had two episodes of pneumococcal sepsis. Ultrasound shows an atrophic, densely echogenic spleen. The peripheral smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies, and vaccination with the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine produces a poor antibody response. He later develops sepsis with Streptococcus pneumoniae despite appropriate penicillin prophylaxis.
question: Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to encapsulated organisms?

options.text: Absent thymic negative selection of T cells
Loss of medullary cord plasma cells in the lymph nodes
Loss of splenic marginal-zone B cells and red pulp macrophage clearance of opsonized organisms
Deficiency of M cells in Peyer patches
Deficiency of complement C3 synthesis by the liver

explanation_correct: Repeated vaso-occlusive infarction of the spleen in sickle cell disease produces autosplenectomy, so the organ is atrophic and nonfunctional. The splenic marginal zone contains B cells specialized for T cell-independent responses to polysaccharide capsules, and the red pulp contains macrophages that clear opsonized encapsulated organisms from the blood; both functions are lost. This leaves patients vulnerable to fulminant sepsis with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae, which is why vaccination and prophylactic penicillin are essential, and why the peripheral smear shows Howell-Jolly bodies.

explanation_incorrect.A: Thymic negative selection of T cells is intact in sickle cell disease and does not contribute to this organism-specific susceptibility.
explanation_incorrect.B: Nodal medullary plasma cells are not the primary defense against blood-borne encapsulated bacteria, and they are not uniformly lost here.
explanation_incorrect.D: M cells sample antigen in the gut mucosa and are not the reason a child with autosplenectomy cannot clear blood-borne pneumococci.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hepatic C3 synthesis is preserved in sickle cell disease; the defect is loss of splenic filtering and marginal-zone function.

educationalObjective: Functional asplenia in sickle cell disease removes splenic marginal-zone B cell responses and red pulp clearance, causing susceptibility to encapsulated organisms.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 13-year-old boy has 1 week of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Examination shows exudative pharyngitis, palatal petechiae, and bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The complete blood count shows lymphocytosis with many atypical lymphocytes, and a Monospot test is positive. After a basketball game he develops sudden severe left upper quadrant pain, becomes tachycardic, and has rebound tenderness; computed tomography shows a splenic laceration with hemoperitoneum.
question: In this condition, the splenic enlargement results primarily from expansion of which of the following?

options.text: Red pulp sinusoids engorged with sickled erythrocytes
Red pulp cords with extramedullary hematopoiesis
The white pulp, from proliferation of T cells responding to infected B cells

explanation_correct: Epstein-Barr virus infects B lymphocytes through CD21 and drives polyclonal B cell activation, and the white pulp consequently expands with a massive reactive proliferation of CD8+ T cells, the source of the atypical lymphocytes on smear. The enlarged spleen has a thin capsule and is prone to rupture, which is why patients are advised to avoid contact sports for several weeks after infectious mononucleosis. Splenic rupture presents with acute left upper quadrant pain, tachycardia, and hemoperitoneum.

explanation_incorrect.A: Sickled erythrocytes cause autosplenectomy with an atrophic spleen in sickle cell disease, not the acute splenomegaly of mononucleosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Extramedullary hematopoiesis expands the red pulp in myelofibrosis or chronic hemolysis, not in EBV infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Capsular fibrosis occurs in chronic conditions such as congestive splenomegaly and does not drive acute enlargement here.
explanation_incorrect.E: Histiocytic sinus distension is seen in Rosai-Dorfman disease, which does not present with exudative pharyngitis and a positive Monospot test.

educationalObjective: Infectious mononucleosis enlarges the spleen through white pulp T cell proliferation against EBV-infected B cells, creating a risk of splenic rupture.
